tagline: Interest rates, tariffs, China's slowdown, and why your coffee costs more.
why: The economy is the backdrop to everyone's job, rent and investments, and in Hong Kong it's shaped by both the US (through the dollar peg) and mainland China. Economic small talk is about whether things are getting better or worse, interest rates, trade wars, and local issues like retail, tourism and people spending weekends in Shenzhen. You don't need to be an economist, just able to follow the main forces.

essentials.title: Inflation and interest rates
essentials.body: When prices rise fast (inflation), central banks raise rates to cool demand. When the economy slows, they cut. The US Fed's moves ripple worldwide.

essentials.title: GDP and recession
essentials.body: GDP measures the size of an economy. Two quarters of shrinking GDP is a common definition of recession.

essentials.title: Trade and tariffs
essentials.body: Tariffs are taxes on imports. The US raised tariffs dramatically in 2025, especially on China, disrupting supply chains and markets.

essentials.title: China's slowdown
essentials.body: China's economy grew fast for decades but now faces a property crisis, falling prices (deflation), weak consumer spending and youth unemployment.

essentials.title: Hong Kong is a hub
essentials.body: Hong Kong's economy runs on finance, trade, logistics, tourism and property. Its currency is pegged to the US dollar.

essentials.title: Jobs and wages
essentials.body: Employment, wage growth and the cost of living are what people feel. AI's effect on jobs is a new worry.

names.name: The Federal Reserve
names.what: The US central bank; its rate decisions move global markets and HK rates.

names.name: HKMA

names.name: Donald Trump

names.name: Xi Jinping
names.what: China's leader, steering policy toward tech and self-reliance.

names.what: International Monetary Fund; publishes global growth forecasts.

names.name: Evergrande
names.what: The Chinese developer whose collapse symbolised China's property crisis; ordered liquidated by a Hong Kong court in 2024.

names.name: John Maynard Keynes

timeline.event: Hong Kong dollar pegged to the US dollar.
China joins the WTO and becomes the world's factory.
Inflation hits 40-year highs in the US; rates rise fast.
Hong Kong reopens; China's property crisis deepens.
Sweeping US tariffs; China exports record trade surpluses elsewhere; Fed cuts rates.

now.headline: Fed set to hike again
now.detail: October CPI rose 0.4% on the month; markets price about a 90% chance of a 25bp hike on 8-9 December under Chair Kevin Warsh.

now.headline: A heavy data week
now.detail: China's October activity data lands on 16 November, with forecasts of just +0.8% for retail sales and +5.3% for industrial output. US retail sales follow on Tuesday and the Fed's minutes on Wednesday.

now.headline: Japan likely to hike too
now.detail: A Reuters poll has the Bank of Japan raising rates to 1.50% at its 17-18 December meeting; Japan's Q3 GDP was expected to show barely any growth.

now.headline: Hong Kong grows 5.2%
now.detail: HK's Q3 GDP grew 5.2% year on year, the fastest since 2023, and the government raised its 2026 forecast to 4.8%.

now.headline: AI exports boom
now.detail: Hong Kong's real goods exports jumped 30% in Q3 on demand for AI-related electronics.

now.headline: Yields above 5%
now.detail: The US 10-year yield is about 5.15%, pushing up borrowing costs, including HIBOR-linked mortgages here.

local.headline: Northbound spending
local.detail: Hong Kongers go to Shenzhen on weekends for cheaper food, shopping and massages, hurting local restaurants and retail.

local.headline: Tourism has changed
local.detail: Mainland tourists returned but spend less on luxury and more on experiences.

local.headline: Budget deficit
local.detail: Hong Kong ran large deficits as land sales fell, leading to spending cuts.

local.headline: Talent schemes
local.detail: The Top Talent Pass Scheme brought in many new residents, mostly from the mainland.

local.headline: Finance rebound
local.detail: A strong IPO market and stock rally in 2025 boosted the finance sector.

debates.question: Do tariffs work?
debates.sides: Supporters say they protect jobs; critics say consumers pay more and trade partners retaliate.

debates.question: Is Hong Kong's best time behind it?
debates.sides: Optimists cite finance and the Greater Bay Area; pessimists cite emigration and retail decline.

debates.question: Will AI take jobs?
debates.sides: Some see productivity gains; others see displacement of white-collar work.

debates.question: Should HK keep the peg?
debates.sides: It brings stability but imports US rates that may not suit Hong Kong.
